title: How big is three quarters times two fifths?
description: Three quarters is multiplied by two fifths. Both numbers and the product are then written with twenty as the bottom, so they can be lined up and compared. Keeko raises the doubt that multiplying always makes a number bigger.
teaching_notes: One idea: when both numbers are between zero and one, the product is less than both of them. Watch for students who believe that multiplying always makes a number bigger.

source: Multiply 3/4 × 2/5 and compare the product with both numbers
video_script.why: A learner sees that a product of two numbers between zero and one is less than both of them.
video_script.substitution: the numbers of the book's own second situation, three quarters and two fifths
video_script.anchor: three quarters, two fifths and their product, each written as twentieths
video_script.wrong_move: believes multiplying always makes a number bigger
video_script.payoff_line: Three quarters times two fifths is three tenths, which is less than both numbers

final_answer.spoken: three tenths, which is less than both numbers

video_script.fraction_reading: three quarters, two fifths, six twentieths, three tenths, fifteen twentieths, eight twentieths
maths_rules: 3/4 is less than 1 and 2/5 is less than 1
6/20 is less than 8/20 and less than 15/20
6/20 = 3/10 after dividing top and bottom by 2
video_script.design: Three bars of equal length split into twenty parts, showing fifteen, eight and six parts.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the numbers 3/4 and 2/5 with a times sign between them

marks.pose: the two fractions arrive with a times sign between them
marks.ask: a question mark glows beside the product

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the size of a product.
<bookmark mark='pose'/>Multiply three quarters by two fifths, and compare the product with both numbers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will the product be greater or smaller than the two numbers?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a number line from 0 to 1 with a bar for each fraction; one marked at the right end

marks.sort: the number line arrives with one marked
marks.part: the stretch from zero to one is shaded
marks.same: two bars are cut into the same number of equal parts

narration: <bookmark mark='sort'/>The size of a product depends on where each number sits.
<bookmark mark='part'/>A fraction between zero and one is only a part of a whole.
<bookmark mark='same'/>To compare fractions, we can write them with the same bottom.

marks.given: the two fractions are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are three quarters and two fifths.

beats.on_screen: To find: 3/4 × 2/5, and how it compares with 3/4 and 2/5

marks.find: the words To find and the product are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to multiply them and compare the product with both numbers.

beats.on_screen: 3/4 < 1 because 3 < 4; 2/5 < 1 because 2 < 5; both are between 0 and 1

marks.cmp: each fraction is placed against the mark for one

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step one, compare each number with one.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Three quarters is less than one, because its top is less than its bottom.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Two fifths is less than one for the same reason.

marks.mult: the tops are joined by a times sign over the bottoms

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step two, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms, three times two over four times five.

beats.on_screen: 3/4 = 15/20, 2/5 = 8/20, product = 6/20; the three bars show 15, 8 and 6 parts out of 20; 6/20 < 8/20 < 15/20

marks.twent: the three bars are cut into twenty equal parts each
marks.first: the bars for three quarters and two fifths are shaded
marks.prod: the bar for the product is shaded and is the shortest

narration: <bookmark mark='twent'/>Step three, write both numbers and the product with twenty below, so we can compare them.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Three quarters is fifteen twentieths, and two fifths is eight twentieths.
<bookmark mark='prod'/>The product, three times two over four times five, is six twentieths.

marks.low: six twentieths is divided top and bottom by two

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Three quarters times two fifths is three tenths, which is less than both numbers.
<bookmark mark='low'/>Six twentieths, in lowest form, is three tenths.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: multiplying makes bigger; a whole bar with two fifths of it shaded, which is shorter than the whole bar

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble says multiplying makes a number bigger
marks.slip: two fifths of a bar is shaded and is shorter than the whole
marks.fix: three quarters of a bar shrinks to a part of that bar

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks multiplying always makes a number bigger, so the product is bigger than both numbers.
<bookmark mark='slip'/>But two fifths of a whole is less than the whole.
Taking a part of three quarters leaves less than three quarters.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>A number between zero and one shrinks the number it multiplies.
